rulings.reason: First-person language chiefly identifies a testimonial or feature format rather than measuring reader interest itself. The reporting approach behind it can also provide genuine human perspective.
Explainer labels are editorial-format markers rather than substantive evidence of what readers actually choose to read. The underlying analytical work can nevertheless produce genuine understanding.
Scare quotes measure a punctuation and hedging convention, not substantive evidence about readership. Their upstream cause may include careful qualification that improves accuracy.
Reader-addressing questions are rhetorical templates rather than direct evidence about actual clicking behavior. They may also arise from genuinely useful service or explainer journalism.
